title: The Middle Ages in Popular Culture

sections.note: SP27 ENGL 202 / CWL 253 / MDVL 201 - Medieval Literature and Culture - Carson Koepke - In this course, we will explore the literary and cultural diversity of the Middle Ages by reading and analyzing narratives from Africa, Asia, Europe, and Mesoamerica around the turn of the first millennium. We will experience how medieval peoples thought about physical and metaphysical travel, how they retold epic myths and origin stories, and how the genre of the medieval romance laid the foundations for the modern novel. Readings (in Modern English translation) will be sourced from a wide variety of religious and linguistic traditions, including Old English, Arabic, Coptic, Chinese, Persian, Japanese, Old Norse, and K'iche' Mayan. As we read, we will work to place narratives like "Beowulf" and "The Tale of Genji" within their wider cultural contexts while also thinking critically about what features and practices unite literature across cultures.
This section is for Undergraduate students.

SP27 ENGL / MDVL 514 - Seminar in Medieval Literature - Carson Koepke - Reconstructing Old English in the Long Seventeenth Century - This iteration of ENGL 514 is an Old English reception course based in the antiquarian, religious, and philological scholarship of the late sixteenth century through the early eighteenth, from Archbishop Matthew Parker and Franciscus Junius to George Hickes and the Elstob siblings. We will read from the first printings of Old English literature and examine these editions and their paratexts through multiple sessions at the RBML. In a sense, we will attempt to recreate the earliest post-medieval environments for scholars and students to learn Old English and read its literature, and we will interrogate their methods by critically engaging with the works they left behind. Topics of study will include the use of early medieval England's literary output as historical evidence for an independent English Church, the (mis)interpretation of Old English as a daughter of the Gothic language, and the mining of primary sources to reconstruct England's political and legal history prior to the Norman Conquest.
